title: Handling Employee Misconduct May Seem Obvious Until It Isn't
author: Kurt Mueller
source: Kurt Mueller's Subscriber Insider Digest (kurtmueller.substack.com), August 15, 2026
summary: This is Kurt Mueller's weekly Subscriber Insider Digest, a curated roundup combining his own leadership-development notes with links to several other pieces on classifying employee misconduct, identifying personal strengths, self-investment discipline, and communication. The digest's own substantive contribution is Mueller's 'Noted' section on incentives, drawn from his work with leadership practitioners, which argues that during disruptive organizational change, informal incentives (what gets attention, resources, recognition, and protection) reveal what an organization actually values far more reliably than official announcements. He offers a practical diagnostic: when a team's behavior looks inconsistent with stated goals, a leader should audit the incentive structure before assuming a communication or motivation problem. The digest closes with a Warren Bennis quote distinguishing managers ('do things right') from leaders ('do the right things'), tying the incentive-auditing framework back to a broader theme of situational, intentional leadership that runs through the issue's linked pieces on self-investment and communication.
points: Mueller's core original contribution is a diagnostic habit: when official messaging and actual behavior diverge during change, audit the incentive structure (what gets rewarded, resourced, and protected) before assuming a communication failure.

He supplies four specific stakeholder questions leaders should ask before defining any deliverable: what outcome the person is accountable for, how their success is judged, what risk concerns them, and what pressure they are under.

He identifies 'mixed incentives' (rewarding individual results while demanding collaboration, for example) as a common, self-inflicted cause of inconsistent team behavior that leaders often misdiagnose as a people problem.
The digest frames self-investment as a judgment discipline rather than a spending rule, proposing the test of whether a purchase will still feel valuable three months later.
The issue closes on the classic Bennis distinction between managers who 'do things right' and leaders who 'do the right things,' using it to frame the digest's leadership-development notes.
quotes: Key Idea: Incentives motivate behavior by shaping anticipated consequences. People naturally consider: What will happen if I do this? What will happen if I do not? What will I gain, protect, risk, or lose?

During disruptive change, official messages may tell you what the organization intends. But incentives often reveal what people believe actually matters. Notice what receives attention, resources, recognition, and protection.

Here is what you need to find out first: What outcome is this stakeholder accountable for? How will their success be judged? What risk are they concerned about? What pressure are they currently experiencing?

Mixed incentives create mixed behavior. Is your team being told to innovate while being punished for mistakes? Is your project leader being asked to collaborate while being rewarded for individual results?
When inconsistent behavior is detected, examine whether the incentives are inconsistent first.
Managers are people who do things right, and leaders are people who do the right things." (Warren Bennis)
A useful question to ask before buying something: What are the odds I'll think this is more valuable 3 months from now than I do today?
